questions.question: Design a social media feed like Twitter or Instagram timeline.
questions.title: Design a Social Media Feed (Twitter/Instagram Timeline)
questions.direct_answer: Use a **hybrid fan-out model**: **fan-out-on-write** (push) for users with under ~10K followers — the post is written into each follower's pre-computed timeline in Redis sorted sets at publish time. **Fan-out-on-read** (pull) for celebrity accounts — the post stays in storage and is **merged into the timeline at read time**. A **Feed Service** combines a follower's pre-computed feed with the latest celebrity posts they follow, applies a **ranking model** (engagement signals, recency, affinity), and returns a paginated, ranked timeline. Store posts in **Cassandra** (partitioned by user_id), follower graph in a **graph DB or sharded relational store**, and pre-computed timelines in **Redis sorted sets**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Fan-out strategy under follower-graph skew, timeline storage choice, ranking vs chronological ordering, caching at scale, and handling celebrity accounts.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Pure fan-out-on-write for everyone (write amplification on celebrities) or pure fan-out-on-read (merging hundreds of follow lists per request kills latency).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Justify the hybrid threshold quantitatively, explain how ranking replaces strict chronology, address consistency on unfollow/block mid-scroll, and call out how the feed service degrades under hot traffic.

sections.title: Framing the Problem and What Makes This Hard
sections.content:
A social media feed sounds like "join posts with follows, sort by time." The reasons that doesn't work at scale:

- **Follower graph is heavily skewed** — most users have under 1,000 followers; a tiny fraction have tens of millions. The architecture that's right for the median is wrong for the long tail.
- **Read:write ratio is huge** — maybe 1,000:1. A post is read far more times than it's written. Architecture biases hard toward read-path optimization.
- **Latency is unforgiving** — timeline open is the home screen. Sub-200 ms for the first page is table stakes.
- **Ranking, not just chronology** — modern feeds aren't reverse-chronological; they apply ML-driven relevance ranking. Storage and serving need to support feature-rich post objects.
- **Mid-scroll consistency** — if I unfollow someone or block someone while scrolling, do their posts disappear from my next page? "Yes" requires expensive re-validation; "no" is acceptable for most products.
- **Celebrity write amplification** — fan-out-on-write pushes each post into every follower's timeline. At 50M followers, that's 50M writes for one tweet. Naive design melts.
- **Real-time delivery for active sessions** — if someone you follow posts while you're scrolling, you expect the new post indicator to appear within seconds.

The central architectural choice: **how do we materialize the timeline so reads are O(constant)** while keeping write cost manageable across the spectrum from a 5-follower account to a 100M-follower one.

sections.title: Clarifying Questions I'd Ask First
sections.content:
**Functional**
- Timeline contents: text posts, images, videos, all of the above?
- **Reverse-chronological or ranked**? (Modern → ranked.)
- **Replies, retweets/reposts, quote-posts** — are these separate post types in the feed?
- **Real-time updates** while user is viewing the feed?
- **Notifications** when someone you follow posts?
- **Multiple feed surfaces**: home, profile, hashtag, explore?

**Non-functional**
- **DAU and posts/day** — drives capacity.
- **Median follower count and tail** — drives fan-out strategy.
- **Latency budget** — sub-200 ms p99 typical.
- **Geographic distribution** — multi-region active-active?
- **Feed depth** — how far back can users scroll?

**Out-of-scope clarifications**
- I'd ask whether DMs, stories, search, and explore are in scope. They're separate systems built on top of the same data.

sections.title: Assumptions I'm Locking In
sections.content:
- **500M DAU**, **2B total users**.
- **400M posts/day** average, peak 4× during major events.
- **Median user has 200 followers**; 99.9th percentile celebrity has 50M+ followers.
- **Celebrity threshold = 10K followers** for the hybrid fan-out boundary.
- **Average user follows 300 accounts**, so the merge-on-read for celebrities is bounded.
- **Feed = 200 most recent ranked items** in cache; deeper scroll triggers DB fallback.
- **Ranked feed**, not strictly chronological. Ranking is computed at read time (light) plus an offline ML pipeline for heavy features.
- **Sub-200 ms p99** for `GET /home_timeline?cursor=...` first page.
- **Eventual consistency on follow/unfollow** for feed contents — acceptable seconds-to-minutes lag.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Capacity Estimate
sections.content:
**Throughput**

- Posts: 400M/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ **4,600/sec average, 18,000/sec peak**.
- Feed reads: 500M DAU each opening the feed ~10×/day = 5B reads/day ≈ **58,000/sec average, ~250,000/sec peak**.
- **Read:write ratio ≈ 13:1** (compute) but **fan-out-on-write multiplies the effective write load by average follower count**.

**Fan-out on write — the math that forces hybrid**

- Median user (200 followers): 200 timeline writes per post.
- Celebrity (50M followers): 50M writes per post. At 10 such posts/min, that's **500M writes/min from one user** — obviously infeasible.
- Total writes if pure fan-out-on-write at 4,600 posts/sec × average 1,000 followers ≈ **4.6M timeline writes/sec**. Possible but expensive.
- With celebrity exclusion (only fan out for < 10K followers), drops to ~**1.5M timeline writes/sec** — manageable.

**Storage**

- Per post: ~1 KB (text + metadata; media in object storage).
- 400M/day × 1 KB = **400 GB/day** of post rows. Cassandra easily.
- Pre-computed timelines in Redis: 500M DAU × 200 entries × 50 bytes = **5 TB Redis** — sharded across ~50 large nodes.

**Conclusion**: post-storage is small; the heavy lifting is timeline materialization in Redis and the ranking compute on read.

sections.title: API Contract
sections.content:
Two read endpoints (home and profile) and a write endpoint:

```http
POST /api/v1/posts
Authorization: Bearer ...
{
  "text": "hello world",
  "media_refs": ["s3://..."],
  "reply_to": null
}

201 Created
{
  "post_id": "01HW...",
  "author_id": "u_99",
  "created_at": "2026-04-21T10:00:00Z"
}
```

Home timeline (the hot read):

```http
GET /api/v1/timeline/home?cursor={opaque}&limit=20

200 OK
{
  "items": [
    {
      "post_id": "01HW...",
      "author": {"id":"u_42","name":"Alice","avatar_url":"..."},
      "text": "...",
      "media": [...],
      "engagement": {"likes":42,"replies":3,"reposts":1},
      "viewer_state": {"liked":false,"reposted":false},
      "created_at": "...",
      "rank_score": 0.87
    },
    ...
  ],
  "next_cursor": "opaque-token"
}
```

Profile timeline (chronological, no ranking):

```http
GET /api/v1/timeline/user/{user_id}?cursor=...&limit=20
```

Real-time updates over WebSocket or SSE:

```
GET /api/v1/timeline/home/stream    (long-lived)

event: new_post_available
data: {"new_count": 12}
```

sections.title: Data Model
sections.content:
**Posts** in Cassandra (partition by author_id, clustering by post_id descending):

```cql
CREATE TABLE posts (
    author_id    bigint,
    post_id      timeuuid,
    text         text,
    media_refs   list<text>,
    reply_to     timeuuid,
    created_at   timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((author_id), post_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (post_id DESC);
```

Profile timeline = single partition scan; perfect.

**Follower graph** — two tables for the two access patterns:

```cql
CREATE TABLE followers (
    user_id     bigint,           -- who is being followed
    follower_id bigint,
    followed_at timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), follower_id)
);

CREATE TABLE following (
    user_id     bigint,           -- who is doing the following
    followee_id bigint,
    followed_at timestamp,
    PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), followee_id)
);
```

Denormalized; both updated transactionally on follow/unfollow via batched mutations.

**Engagement counters** in Redis (per-post atomic counters):

```
KEY: post:01HW...:counts → {likes: 42, replies: 3, reposts: 1}
```

Flushed back to a per-post row in Cassandra periodically.

**Pre-computed home timeline** in Redis sorted sets:

```
KEY:   timeline:{user_id}
TYPE:  ZSET
MEMBER: post_id
SCORE:  rank_score (or timestamp for chronological tier)
MAX SIZE: 200 entries (oldest evicted)
```

**Celebrity post cache** — latest 100 posts per celebrity, in Redis:

```
KEY: celebrity:{user_id}:recent
TYPE: LIST (newest first, capped at 100)
```

Relationships:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ POSTS : authors
    USERS ||--o{ FOLLOWERS : followed_by
    USERS ||--o{ FOLLOWING : follows
    POSTS ||--o{ ENGAGEMENT : receives
    USERS {
        bigint user_id PK
        string handle
        bigint follower_count
        bool is_celebrity
    }
    POSTS {
        bigint author_id FK
        timeuuid post_id PK
        text body
        timestamp created_at
    }
    FOLLOWERS {
        bigint user_id FK
        bigint follower_id FK
        timestamp followed_at
    }
    FOLLOWING {
        bigint user_id FK
        bigint followee_id FK
    }
```

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
Two main paths: **publish** (write, with hybrid fan-out) and **read** (assemble + rank + return). ```mermaid flowchart TB Client([Client App]) LB[Load Balancer] PostSvc[Post Service
create + persist] Kafka{{Kafka
posts.created}} FanOut[Fan-Out Service
hybrid policy] GraphSvc[Graph Service
follower lookup] FeedSvc[Feed Service
read + merge + rank] Ranker[Ranking Engine
features + model] Cassandra[(Cassandra
posts, graph)] Timelines[(Redis
timelines + celeb cache)] Hydration[Hydration Service
author + counts] Stream[Real-time Stream
WebSocket / SSE] Client -->|POST /posts| LB LB --> PostSvc PostSvc --> Cassandra PostSvc --> Kafka Kafka --> FanOut FanOut --> GraphSvc FanOut -->|<10K followers| Timelines FanOut -.>|>=10K celebrity| Timelines PostSvc --> Stream Client -->|GET /timeline| LB LB --> FeedSvc FeedSvc --> Timelines FeedSvc --> GraphSvc FeedSvc --> Cassandra FeedSvc --> Ranker FeedSvc --> Hydration Hydration --> Cassandra Hydration --> Timelines classDef edge fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6 classDef svc fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e classDef store fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef bus fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b class LB,Stream edge class PostSvc,FanOut,FeedSvc,Ranker,GraphSvc,Hydration svc class Cassandra,Timelines store class Kafka bus ``` **Publish path:** Post Service writes to Cassandra and emits to Kafka. Fan-Out Service consumes; for non-celebrities, pushes post_id into each follower's timeline ZSET. For celebrities, only updates `celebrity:{user_id}:recent`. Real-time stream notifies actively-connected followers. **Read path:** Feed Service pulls the user's pre-computed timeline ZSET, fetches recent posts from each celebrity they follow, merges, ranks, hydrates author info and engagement counts, returns paginated.

sections.title: Hybrid Fan-Out — The Central Decision
sections.content:
**Threshold = 10K followers** (tunable based on production data).

**Why this number** — below 10K, fan-out-on-write costs ~10K small Redis ZADDs per post (a few hundred ms total, fine async). Above 10K, the cost grows linearly while the read-side merge cost stays bounded by `following_count` (which has a different distribution).

**Publish flow:**

```
for each post by author A:
    if A.follower_count < 10_000:
        for follower in graph.followers_of(A):       # paginated fetch
            redis.zadd("timeline:" + follower, score, post_id)
            evict_oldest_if_over_200(follower)
    else:
        redis.lpush("celebrity:" + A + ":recent", post_id)
        ltrim(100)
```

**Read flow:**

```
def build_home_timeline(user_id, cursor):
    pre = redis.zrevrange("timeline:" + user_id, 0, 200)         # pushed posts
    celebs = graph.celebrity_followees_of(user_id)               # bounded list
    pulled = []
    for c in celebs:
        pulled += redis.lrange("celebrity:" + c + ":recent", 0, 20)
    candidates = dedup(pre + pulled)
    ranked = ranker.score(user_id, candidates)
    return paginate(ranked, cursor, limit=20)
```

**Why the threshold isn't binary in practice** — some implementations use a **tier system**: tiny (<1K, push), normal (1K–10K, push), big (10K–100K, push but with delay queue), celebrity (>100K, pull). The deeper you tier, the better load smoothing.

**Edge case — a non-celebrity becomes a celebrity overnight** — follower count crosses threshold; we stop fan-out-on-write but their existing pushed entries are still in followers' timelines. Read path naturally picks up new pulled entries; eventual consistency converges in minutes.

sections.title: Ranking and the Read-Time Pipeline
sections.content:
Modern feeds aren't reverse-chronological. Ranking blends:

- **Recency** (decaying score)
- **Affinity** (how often you interact with the author)
- **Engagement signals** (likes/replies/reposts so far)
- **Content type** (text vs photo vs video — user preference learned)
- **Diversity penalty** (don't show 5 posts from the same author in a row)

**Lightweight read-time scoring** — rank candidates with a simple linear/logistic model on cached features. Keeps the read budget under 50ms.

**Heavy ML model** — runs offline (every few hours) and produces a per-user candidate-quality cache that the read-time scorer consults. Avoids running a deep model on every page load.

**Why not pure chronological?**

- Users open the feed once a day, see their friend's lunch photo from 18 hours ago. Bad experience.
- Ranking surfaces the most relevant content first, dramatically improves time-spent and engagement.
- Trade-off: harder to reason about "why am I seeing this" — product needs an explainability layer.

**Hydration** — the timeline ZSET stores only post_ids. The Hydration Service expands each into a full post object with author info, engagement counts, and viewer-relative state ("have I liked this?"). Hydration is parallelized and aggressively cached.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design of the Feed Service
Storage Choice and Sharding
sections.content:
**Cassandra for posts** — partition by `author_id` so a profile timeline is a single-partition scan. Sharded across hundreds of nodes; replication factor 3 with `LOCAL_QUORUM`.

**Cassandra for follower graph** — same access pattern fit. For very large follower lists (celebrity 50M+ followers), the partition exceeds Cassandra's recommended size (~100MB). Mitigations: bucket by hash of follower_id (logical sub-partitions), or move large-follower-count users to a graph DB (Neo4j, JanusGraph). At extreme scale (Twitter), this is the FlockDB approach.

**Redis for timelines** — ZSETs are cheap, sorted operations are O(log n), TTL handles cleanup. Sharded Redis Cluster keyed by user_id. Memory cost ~5 TB across cluster.

**Why not put posts in Redis too?** Cost — 400 GB/day of post data would balloon Redis. Posts go in cheap durable storage; only the small timeline indices stay in Redis.

**Why not relational for the graph?** PostgreSQL JOINs across follow tables don't scale; recursive lookups (follower-of-follower) are even worse. Graph access patterns favor wide-column or graph DBs.

sections.title: Caching, Hot Posts, and Mid-Scroll Consistency
sections.content:
**Layered cache:**

- **L1**: per-FeedService-instance Caffeine cache for hydrated FeedItems (1-minute TTL) — absorbs repeat hits.
- **L2**: Redis hydration cache for `(post_id, viewer_id) → FeedItem` (5-minute TTL).
- **L3**: pre-computed timeline ZSET (the source for pushed posts).
- **Origin**: Cassandra.

**Hot-post problem** — a viral celebrity post might appear in 50M home timelines being read simultaneously. Hydration cache makes this nearly free; the underlying post row is read once, served millions of times.

**Mid-scroll consistency on unfollow/block:**

- ZSET still contains old entries from the unfollowed author for up to ~200 entries.
- Two options:
  - **Strict**: read-time filter against the user's current following list (extra cost, ~5ms).
  - **Relaxed**: tolerate up to one timeline page of stale entries; future entries naturally exclude.
- Most products choose **relaxed for unfollow**, **strict for block** (block must take effect immediately for safety).

**Cold-cache problem on Redis restart:**

- Pre-warm timelines for top 10% of DAU from a daily snapshot.
- For remaining users, first request triggers a rebuild from scratch — read posts from Cassandra for each followee, populate ZSET. Slow (200ms) but correct.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Resilience
sections.content:
**Fan-Out Service crash mid-distribution**

- Kafka offset uncommitted → another instance picks up the post.
- Redis ZADD is idempotent (set semantics) — duplicate ADD is a no-op.
- Worst case: a few followers' timelines get the post written twice (still appears once due to ZSET dedup).

**Cassandra node failure**

- LOCAL_QUORUM tolerates 1 of 3 replicas down.
- Read path falls over to surviving replicas with elevated latency.

**Redis timeline shard down**

- Affected users see degraded feed: only celebrity-pulled posts plus a fallback Cassandra-based timeline rebuild.
- Latency spikes from ~50ms to ~500ms for affected slice.
- Sharded Redis Cluster failover promotes replica within ~30 seconds.

**Ranking service slow**

- Ranker has a 30ms internal timeout.
- Fallback: chronological order of candidates with simple recency decay.
- User sees a worse but functional feed; no error.

**Kafka backlog (publish queue lag)**

- Posts persist immediately to Cassandra; profile timeline is correct.
- Home timelines lag — follower sees the post a few seconds late.
- Acceptable; we monitor `kafka.lag.posts.created` and alert above 30 seconds.

**Celebrity post hot key**

- 50M concurrent reads hitting `celebrity:{X}:recent` could melt one Redis shard.
- Mitigation: in-process Caffeine cache on Feed Service instances absorbs the bulk; Redis hit rate stays low for hot keys.

sections.title: Observability and Security
sections.content:
**Metrics**

- `timeline.build.latency` p50/p95/p99 — SLO p99 < 200ms.
- `timeline.cache.hit_rate` (target > 90% for hydration).
- `fanout.lag` — time from post creation to all followers' timelines updated.
- `celebrity.read.parallelism` — number of celebrity caches fetched per request.
- `ranker.latency` and `ranker.fallback_rate`.
- `redis.shard.utilization` — spot hot shards.

**Tracing**

- Trace ID flows from API → FeedService → (parallel: timeline read + celebrity reads + ranker + hydration). Helps diagnose which sub-step blew the latency budget.

**Security and abuse**

- **Block list filtering** at read time — strict; never show a blocked user's content.
- **Shadow ban** support — some posts visible only to author, not in others' timelines (anti-abuse).
- **Rate limit on post creation** to prevent spam (e.g., 300 posts/hour per user).
- **Content moderation** runs asynchronously; flagged posts removed from caches via tombstone propagation.
- **Authentication and per-user data scoping** — no cross-user data leakage in hydration responses (e.g., `viewer_state.liked` correctly scoped).

sections.title: Trade-offs and What I'd Change at 10× Scale
sections.content:
**At 10× scale (5B DAU, 4B posts/day):**

- **Timeline DB instead of Redis ZSETs** — Twitter built Manhattan; Meta built TAO. Purpose-built timeline storage is cheaper and faster than Redis at extreme scale.
- **Per-region active-active** with timeline replication; cross-region follower lookups expensive enough to keep regional.
- **Edge ranking** — push the lightweight scorer to CDN/edge compute; Feed Service returns candidate sets only.
- **Pre-fetched feeds** — push next page to client during read so scroll is instant.

**What I'd reconsider:**

- **Hybrid threshold** — 10K is a guess. Production data on per-user write cost vs read cost would calibrate. Some platforms use 100K, some go fully pull-based for everyone above 1K.
- **Pure ranked vs chronological-on-demand** — some products offer a chronological toggle; supporting both means storing two timelines or computing one from the other on demand.

**What I rejected and why:**

- **Pure fan-out-on-write** — melts on celebrities (50M writes per post). Non-starter.
- **Pure fan-out-on-read** — a user following 1,000 accounts means 1,000 storage reads per timeline open. Latency budget exceeded; cost balloons.
- **Storing pre-rendered HTML feed in cache** — violates separation of data and presentation; clients render UI from typed FeedItems; a single bad row corrupts the whole cached page.
- **Computing rank at write time** — ranking depends on viewer; can't precompute one score per post.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hybrid fan-out at 10K-follower threshold** — push for the long tail, pull for celebrities. The merge happens at read time.
- **Pre-computed timelines in Redis sorted sets** keyed by user_id — reads are O(constant) for the pushed portion.
- **Celebrity cache (recent posts per celebrity)** is the pull-side complement — small, hot, easy to cache.
- **Cassandra for posts and follower graph** — partition keys match access patterns (author_id for posts, user_id for follow lists).
- **Read-time ranking** with a lightweight model on cached features; heavy ML runs offline and feeds candidate-quality scores into the read path.
- **Hydration as a separate cached step** — timeline ZSETs store post_ids only; full FeedItem is hydrated on demand and aggressively cached.
- **Eventual consistency on follow/unfollow** is acceptable; **block is enforced strictly at read time**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Clarifying questions I'd ask first**

- Reverse-chronological or ranked feed?
- Replies, reposts, quote-posts — separate post types in the feed?
- Real-time updates while user is viewing?
- Multiple feed surfaces (home, profile, hashtag)?
- Acceptable consistency on unfollow — strict or eventual?

**Assumptions for this design**

500 million DAU, 2 billion total users, 400 million posts a day, peak 4× during major events. Median user has ~200 followers; 99.9th-percentile celebrity has 50 million plus. We pick a 10K-follower threshold for the hybrid boundary. Sub-200-millisecond p99 for the home timeline first page. Ranked, not strictly chronological.

**Quick capacity check**

- Posts: ~4,600/sec average, 18,000/sec peak
- Reads: ~58,000/sec average, 250,000/sec peak
- Pure fan-out-on-write would cost 4.6 million timeline writes/sec on average and tens of millions on a celebrity post — doesn't work
- With celebrity exclusion, fan-out drops to ~1.5 million writes/sec — manageable
- Storage: 400 GB/day of posts, 5 TB Redis for timelines

**The central decision — hybrid fan-out**

- Authors with under 10K followers: fan-out-on-write — each post written into every follower's timeline ZSET in Redis
- Authors with 10K+: fan-out-on-read — the post sits in a celebrity-recent cache; followers pull at read time
- The 10K number balances write cost (linear in follower count) against read merge cost (linear in follow count)
- A non-celebrity becoming a celebrity overnight is handled gracefully by eventual consistency — we just stop pushing for them; the read path picks up new entries via the celebrity cache

**High-level shape**

- Publish: Post Service writes to Cassandra, emits to Kafka; Fan-Out Service consumes and applies the hybrid policy
- Read: Feed Service reads pre-computed timeline ZSET, fetches celebrity-recent caches in parallel, dedupes, ranks, hydrates author and engagement, returns paginated
- Real-time: post publish notifies actively-connected followers via WebSocket/SSE

**Data model**

- Cassandra `posts` partitioned by `author_id`, clustered by `post_id` descending — profile timeline is one partition scan
- Cassandra `followers` and `following` tables for graph (denormalized; both written on follow/unfollow)
- Redis ZSETs `timeline:{user_id}` capped at 200 entries
- Redis lists `celebrity:{user_id}:recent` capped at 100 entries
- Engagement counters in Redis, periodically flushed to Cassandra

**Read path — step by step**

- Pull pushed posts from `timeline:{user_id}` ZSET (200 candidates)
- Look up celebrity followees, fetch their recent posts in parallel
- Merge and dedupe
- Rank with a lightweight scorer using cached ML features (offline-trained model produces per-user candidate-quality cache)
- Apply cursor pagination, take 20
- Hydrate: expand post_ids to full FeedItem with author, counts, viewer-relative state — aggressively cached

**LLD — clean abstractions**

- `TimelineStore` interface (RedisTimelineStore impl; can swap for purpose-built timeline DB)
- `FanOutPolicy` extracted — the threshold logic lives in one tested class
- `Ranker` as its own collaborator — swap models with config, A/B test, shadow traffic
- `HydrationService` parallelized with caching
- Feed Service uses parallel streams for celebrity fetch — serial would blow the latency budget

**Caching layers**

- L1 in-process Caffeine for hydrated FeedItems
- L2 Redis hydration cache keyed by (post_id, viewer_id)
- L3 the pre-computed timeline ZSET
- Origin Cassandra
- Hot-post problem (viral post in 50M timelines) handled by L1+L2 — underlying row read once, served millions of times

**Mid-scroll consistency**

- Unfollow: relaxed — stale entries OK for the current page; future entries excluded
- Block: strict — always filter at read time, even at extra cost

**Failure handling**

- Fan-Out crash: Kafka replay; Redis ZADD is idempotent
- Ranker slow: 30ms timeout, fallback to chronological with recency decay
- Redis shard down: degraded feed (celebrity pulls only) until failover (~30s)
- Cassandra node down: LOCAL_QUORUM tolerates 1 of 3
- Cold cache: pre-warm top 10% from snapshot; rebuild on demand for the rest

**Production extras**

- Block-list filtering at read time (strict)
- Shadow ban support for abuse handling
- Rate limit posts per user (300/hour)
- Content moderation async; tombstones propagate to caches
- Distributed tracing across the parallel read fan-out

**At 10× scale**

- Purpose-built timeline DB (Twitter Manhattan, Meta TAO) instead of Redis
- Per-region active-active
- Edge ranking (CDN/edge compute)
- Pre-fetched next page on the client

**Recommendation**

**Hybrid fan-out at a 10K-follower threshold, pre-computed timelines in Redis ZSETs for the long tail, celebrity caches for pull-merge at read time, Cassandra for posts and graph, lightweight read-time ranking backed by an offline-trained candidate-quality model, and aggressive hydration caching** — the same shape Twitter, Instagram, and LinkedIn run today.

Mid-scroll consistency —.
Pure fan-out-on-write for everyone (write amplification on celebrities) or pure fan-out-on-read (merging hundreds of follow lists per request kills latency).

Hybrid fan-out at 10K-follower threshold — push for the long tail, pull for celebrities. The merge happens at read time. Pre-computed timelines in Redis sorted sets keyed by user_id — reads are O(constant) for the pushed portion. Celebrity cache (recent posts per celebrity) is the pull-side complement — small, hot, easy to cache. Cassandra for posts and follower graph — partition keys match access patterns (author_id for posts, user_id for follow lists). Read-time ranking with a lightweight model on cached features; heavy ML runs offline.
